sources.meta: Ngo et al. · 2019 · Časopis lékařů českých 158(3–4):147–150
sources.title: Evaluation of the personalized invitation of Czech citizens to screening programs
sources.finding: In the 2014–2017 evaluation, 22.3% of women attended after their first breast-screening invitation. Response declined with repeated invitations.
sources.limit: Invited women were already overdue. This is neither national coverage nor a randomized estimate of the letter’s effect.

sources.meta: Altová, Lustigová & Kulhánová · 2023 · European Journal of Public Health supplement
sources.title: “I feel healthy, I don’t need to go”: Analysis of the cancer screening barrier
sources.finding: Among breast-screening non-attendees, 29.2% reported absence of symptoms as a reason for not attending.
sources.limit: Abstract-level evidence. Stated reasons were not linked to verified receipt of an insurer’s invitation; they do not establish causation.

sources.title: Participation in cancer screening: inequalities and individual experiences
sources.finding: Qualitative interviews describe relationships with clinicians, difficult previous experiences and attitudes to prevention.
sources.limit: Ten interviews across breast and cervical screening; only five participants were mammography-eligible. Useful for hypotheses, not prevalence estimates.

sources.title: A second timed appointment after missing breast screening
sources.finding: Attendance was approximately 22% with a second fixed appointment versus 12% with an open invitation to book; relative risk 1.81 (95% CI 1.70–1.93).
sources.limit: Assignment used odd/even screening identifiers. English appointment workflows and this missed-appointment cohort differ from Czech insurer-letter recipients.

sources.title: Pre-scheduled appointments in an organized breast-screening programme
sources.finding: Fixed appointments increased participation by 4.4 percentage points among hospital never-attendees, 15.8 among irregular hospital attendees, and 8.3 in a mobile-unit group.
sources.limit: Effects differed by prior attendance and setting. A single average cannot be assumed for Czechia.

sources.meta: Kerrison et al. · 2015 · British Journal of Cancer · 2,240 women
sources.title: Text-message reminders before a first breast-screening appointment
sources.finding: Intention-to-treat attendance increased from 59.1% to 64.4% with a reminder text: +5.3 percentage points.
sources.limit: Only 41% in the intervention group had a mobile number recorded. First invitations with appointments are different from persistent non-attendance.

sources.meta: Ministry of Health / Health Promotion Board · NPHS 2022
sources.title: National Population Health Survey 2022: breast screening and reasons for never screening
sources.finding: Among never-screened women aged 50–69, 40.5% reported feeling healthy without symptoms and 16.9% cited pain. Awareness of mammography was much higher than recent use.
sources.limit: Self-reported reasons in never-screened women; not an experiment and not a study of delivered reminder letters.

sources.title: Breast cancer screening, 2024
sources.finding: 79% of women aged 50–74 reported a mammogram within three years. Among those without one, 32% considered it unnecessary and 20% said a provider did not think it necessary.
sources.limit: Ten provinces, self-report and a three-year window. Reasons do not identify the effect of any specific intervention.

sources.title: Reasons for non-participation in mammography screening
sources.finding: Among 1,494 counselled women, 51.5% reported “grey screening” and 26.6% time problems. The grey-screening category included mammography and other breast examinations.
sources.limit: Selected reachable participants; multiple reasons allowed. Ultrasound, clinical examination and self-examination cannot all be counted as equivalent mammography coverage. Counselling-group comparisons are not an intention-to-treat causal effect.

sources.title: Behavioral Interventions to Improve Breast Cancer Screening Outreach: Two Randomized Clinical Trials
sources.finding: Bulk orders increased three-month completion from 12.7% to 15.4%. Texts added about 2.1–2.5 percentage points. Clinician endorsement alone was not significant (12.5% versus 11.4%).
sources.limit: US health-system patients; 48 randomized patients were excluded from analysis. Ordering, insurance and referral pathways differ from Czech care.

sources.meta: Beauchamp et al. · 2020 · PLOS ONE · two trials
sources.title: Translated letters and in-language calls for Arabic- and Italian-speaking women
sources.finding: Translated letters alone did not significantly improve booking (n=1,032). In the separate phone trial (n=195), 64.2% booked within 14 days versus 6.0% without a call.
sources.limit: Booking, not completed screening. The phone comparison bundled personal contact and language support, so their separate effects are unknown.

sources.title: Mammography screening in the target population
sources.finding: Two-year mammography use among women aged 50–69 was 58.3%; urban 60.5%, rural 41.6%. Use differed substantially by education.
sources.limit: Observational self-report. Rural residence is not a randomized transport intervention; this is not a reminder-response rate.

sources.meta: Lee et al. · online 2025 / 2026 issue · JAMA Internal Medicine · 9,000 women
sources.title: Behavioral interventions added to breast-screening reminders
sources.finding: All groups received mail and three app reminders. Rewards, videos and a hotline did not significantly improve overall uptake; standard reminders achieved 11.2%, hotline 13.8%.
sources.limit: No group without reminders. Previously screened, overdue app users; low engagement with intervention pages. This does not show reminders themselves are ineffective.

sources.title: The effect of mammography pain on repeat participation
sources.finding: Pain was linked to non-return in several studies. The pooled relative risk was 1.34, with an imprecise 95% CI of 0.94–1.91.
sources.limit: The interval includes no association. Pain is a credible experience to address, but this review does not establish that a reassurance leaflet improves attendance.

sources.title: Health-related social needs and mammography use
sources.finding: Median mammography use across jurisdictions was 83.2% among women reporting no adverse social needs versus 65.7% among those reporting three or more.
sources.limit: Cross-sectional associations and jurisdiction medians. US financial barriers cannot simply be transferred to Czech publicly insured screening.

sources.title: Mammography: population coverage, open data
sources.finding: Provides claims-based screening coverage with age, region and time definitions, using specified mammography procedure codes.
sources.limit: Claims coverage is different from a cohort’s response after a letter. Privately paid or otherwise unreported examinations may be absent; establish linkage and claims lag before trial analysis.

sources.title: Changes in organization of screening mammography from July 2026
sources.finding: A screening centre may issue a referral in justified exceptional situations. The usual GP or gynaecologist referral pathway remains.
sources.limit: This is not a universal removal of referral requirements. Operational messaging must reflect the actual policy and centre workflow.

sources.meta: European Commission Initiative on Breast Cancer · online recommendations
sources.title: European breast cancer guidelines: screening participation and informed choice
sources.finding: Recommendations address participation strategies, including appointment and reminder approaches, while preserving understandable information about benefits and harms and informed decisions.
sources.limit: Recommendations have different certainty ratings and target populations. They are not one universal causal effect or a Czech implementation protocol.

sources.title: CONSORT 2025 statement: updated reporting of randomized trials
sources.finding: Requires transparent trial reporting, including prespecified outcomes, allocation, participant flow, sample-size reasoning, analysis populations and effect estimates with precision.
sources.limit: A reporting standard supports credible evaluation; it does not select the best intervention or replace study-specific ethical and statistical planning.

sources.title: Reporting cluster randomized trials
sources.finding: Addresses cluster-level allocation, intracluster correlation, recruitment, sample-size adjustment and analysis appropriate to clustered data.
sources.limit: Woman-level and centre-level trials need different calculations. A large patient count cannot compensate automatically for too few centres.

sources.title: Mammography use and social determinants of health
sources.finding: 80.0% of women aged 50–74 reported mammography within two years in 2023.
sources.limit: Self-report can include diagnostic mammography. Survey response and recall differ from administrative organized-screening counts.

sources.title: BreastScreen Australia: participation indicator
sources.finding: Final participation among women aged 50–74 was 52.4% in 2023–2024.
sources.limit: Programme participation, not all mammography. Do not mix the final 2023–2024 value with preliminary 2024–2025 reporting.

sources.meta: Kang et al. · 2025 · Cancer Research and Treatment 57:28–38
sources.title: Trends in Cancer-Screening Rates in Korea: Findings from the National Cancer Screening Survey, 2004–2023
sources.finding: Recommendation-concordant breast screening was 72.7% in 2023, defined using mammography within two years and an eligibility threshold starting at age 40.
sources.limit: Survey definition and age distribution differ from European programmes. It is not an insurer invitation response.

sources.title: National Population Health Survey 2024
sources.finding: 35.2% of women aged 50–69 reported mammography within two years.
sources.limit: A different survey year from the 2022 barrier questions. Trends and reasons must not be treated as measurements from the same cohort.

sources.title: Barriers and facilitators to breast cancer screening in East Africa
sources.finding: Studies describe knowledge, fear, cost and availability barriers across breast-screening practices.
sources.limit: Mixed self-examination, clinical examination and mammography; only one mammography-focused study. Not an estimate of mammography-letter non-response.

sources.title: Power for a test of two independent proportions
sources.finding: Documents a normal-approximation power calculation using pooled variance under the null and unpooled variance under the alternative.
sources.limit: The report’s calculator uses a closed-form planning approximation. Final sample size should use the prespecified test, design and actual expected rates.

sources.title: Multiple endpoints: controlling false positive conclusions
sources.finding: Explains multiplicity control; equal-weight Bonferroni divides the family’s significance level by its number of comparisons.
sources.limit: Drug-trial guidance is cited for the statistical principle, not as Czech screening regulation. Define the hypothesis family in advance; independent projects need not automatically form one family.

sources.title: Regional availability of screening mammography
sources.finding: A 27 September 2024 snapshot of centres’ published booking waits averaged 21 days nationally, 62 in Karlovy Vary and 11 in Vysočina.
sources.limit: Historical reported booking waits, not current availability or proof that waiting caused non-attendance. Refresh before allocating invitations.

mechanisms.name: Low perceived need
mechanisms.label: Barrier observed; message untested
mechanisms.quote: “I feel well. Why would I go?”
mechanisms.description: Feeling healthy can make screening seem irrelevant. Explain the purpose of checking before symptoms, while preserving a real choice.
mechanisms.evidence: The Czech abstract reports “no symptoms” as a reason in 29.2% of non-attendees. Similar beliefs appear in national Canadian and Singaporean surveys. This supports the hypothesis, not the effectiveness of a rewritten letter. [2] [7] [8]
mechanisms.a: The current balanced invitation, with the usual contact and booking information.
mechanisms.b: The same invitation plus one plain-language explanation: “Screening is intended for women who feel well. Breast changes can be present before symptoms.” Keep the same layout, sender and benefits-and-harms information.
mechanisms.audience: Verified overdue women without symptoms; stratify never-screened versus previously screened.
mechanisms.outcome: Completed eligible mammography within 12 months of randomization; early reads at 3 and 6 months.
mechanisms.check: In a separate pilot, test comprehension of screening’s purpose. If surveyed in the trial, sample both arms equally after the outcome window.
mechanisms.guard: Do not imply that everyone has cancer, or that screening prevents every cancer. Attendance alone does not prove the belief changed.

mechanisms.name: Forgetting & salience
mechanisms.label: Attendance effects in trials
mechanisms.quote: “I intended to book. Then life happened.”
mechanisms.description: An intention may not survive the gap between opening a letter and arranging a visit. A timely second contact may bring the task back into view.
mechanisms.evidence: An English first-invitation trial found +5.3 percentage points with an appointment reminder text. US trials also found small completion gains from texts. The timing and populations differ from Czech overdue recipients. [6] [10]
mechanisms.a: The existing invitation pathway and usual care, with no experimental text.
mechanisms.b: The same pathway plus one concise SMS on day 14, with the existing booking number and a clear next step. Keep wording factual and respect contact preferences.
mechanisms.audience: Randomize on day 14 among women confirmed still unbooked and eligible, with a valid recorded mobile number. Report how many overdue women lack a usable number.
mechanisms.outcome: Completed eligible mammography within 12 months after this day-14 randomization; early reads at 3 and 6 months.
mechanisms.check: Record delivery, booking within 14 further days, and attendance. Undelivered texts stay in the assigned-arm analysis.
mechanisms.guard: Do not compare only women who opened a message. A result in reachable women will not establish effectiveness for those with missing contact details.

mechanisms.name: Booking & referral friction
mechanisms.label: Attendance effects in trials
mechanisms.quote: “I would go if the next step were easier.”
mechanisms.description: Finding a centre, obtaining a referral and calling for a slot can create several opportunities to stop. Test a concrete appointment offer.
mechanisms.evidence: An English trial in previous non-attendees achieved about 22% versus 12% with a second fixed appointment. Belgian effects varied by attendance history. Czech implementation needs its own evaluation. [4] [5]
mechanisms.a: An invitation asking the woman to contact the centre and book, with the usual referral instructions.
mechanisms.b: The same invitation offering a specific appointment, with an easy way to decline or reschedule. Provide accurate referral instructions in both arms; reserve real capacity before sending.
mechanisms.audience: Verified overdue women served by participating centres with available slots; stratify by centre and previous attendance.
mechanisms.outcome: Completed eligible mammography within 12 months of allocation, using the same start date for both arms; early reads at 3 and 6 months.
mechanisms.check: Time to booking, rescheduling, no-shows and unused reserved slots; cost per additional completed screen.
mechanisms.guard: Do not create longer waits for usual-care patients. Czech centres can issue referrals only in justified exceptional situations under the July 2026 change. [17]

mechanisms.name: Fear & discomfort
mechanisms.label: Barrier evidence; intervention uncertain
mechanisms.quote: “I’m worried about the test—and the result.”
mechanisms.description: Pain, vulnerability and uncertainty about a possible recall may matter. Explain the experience honestly and offer a way to ask questions.
mechanisms.evidence: A review linked pain to non-return, but its pooled estimate was imprecise: RR 1.34, 95% CI 0.94–1.91. Czech qualitative work supplies possible experiences, not population frequencies. [14] [3]
mechanisms.a: The usual balanced invitation and existing support contact.
mechanisms.b: The same invitation plus a short “what to expect” panel: compression and discomfort, how to tell the radiographer, and what a recall means. Use the same support contact in both groups.
mechanisms.audience: First-time invitees or a pre-identified anxious cohort; collect any anxiety eligibility measure before allocation in both arms.
mechanisms.outcome: Completed eligible mammography within 12 months; early reads at 3 and 6 months.
mechanisms.check: Understanding and distress in an equally sampled follow-up; complaints and informed refusal as well as attendance.
mechanisms.guard: Do not promise a painless examination or a reassuring result. Test wording with women first; a reassurance message has not been established as effective by the pain review.

mechanisms.name: Practical constraints
mechanisms.label: Associations; local support test needed
mechanisms.description: Transport, caring responsibilities and time off may make an offered visit unusable. Identify the actual constraint before choosing support.
mechanisms.evidence: Brazilian survey use was 41.6% in rural versus 60.5% in urban areas. US social-needs data also show inequalities. Neither establishes the benefit of a Czech transport offer. [12] [15]
mechanisms.a: The standard invitation and ordinary access to existing assistance.
mechanisms.b: The same pathway plus an active offer of pre-arranged transport assistance for this appointment. Test one support service; do not bundle transport, gifts and extended hours.
mechanisms.audience: Women who identify transport as a barrier in the same brief assessment before randomization; available transport and clinical capacity confirmed.
mechanisms.outcome: Completed eligible mammography within 12 months; early reads at 3 and 6 months.
mechanisms.check: Offer delivery, assistance use, travel burden, total support cost and cost per additional completed screen.
mechanisms.guard: Do not infer that rural residence means transport is the problem. A centre-wide change such as evening hours needs a cluster design, rather than this individual A/B plan. [20]

mechanisms.name: Trust & provider connection
mechanisms.label: Mixed evidence; endorsement trial null
mechanisms.quote: “I would like to hear from someone I trust.”
mechanisms.description: A familiar clinician may lend meaning to a recommendation, but a signature alone may do little. Treat this as an open question.
mechanisms.evidence: Czech interviews suggest relationships with clinicians matter. In a US trial, clinician-endorsed outreach did not significantly improve completion: 12.5% versus 11.4%. [3] [10]
mechanisms.a: The current insurer invitation from its usual sender.
mechanisms.b: The identical invitation co-signed by the woman’s own verified GP, with the GP’s authorization. Change only endorsement, not the number of contacts or counselling offered.
mechanisms.audience: Overdue women with an identified participating GP; stratify by practice and prior attendance. Track who has no GP separately.
mechanisms.outcome: Completed eligible mammography within 12 months; early reads at 3 and 6 months.
mechanisms.check: Recognition of sender, trust, complaints and opt-outs in an equally sampled follow-up.
mechanisms.guard: Never imply a personal review that did not happen. A null or small result is plausible; the prior trial does not support promising a large gain.

mechanisms.name: Apparent non-attendance
mechanisms.label: Data-quality mechanism
mechanisms.description: Some apparent non-attendees may have care outside the programme, while others may mistake a different breast test for mammography. Verify rather than assume.
mechanisms.evidence: A German selected sample frequently reported outside or “grey” screening, but the category also included non-mammographic examinations. Claims and programme data have defined capture boundaries. [9] [16]
mechanisms.a: The usual invitation after the same pre-allocation eligibility and claims checks.
mechanisms.b: The identical invitation plus a simple “Already had a mammogram elsewhere?” reply route requesting date and provider, followed by verification.
mechanisms.audience: Women who appear overdue after identical baseline checks. Do not remove people from the analysis merely because they reply in one arm.
mechanisms.outcome: Primary: independently verified correction of screening status within 90 days per woman randomized. Attendance is secondary.
mechanisms.check: Blind reviewers to allocation; distinguish a verified mammogram, another breast test, diagnostic surveillance and an unverified claim. Apply identical verification rules.
mechanisms.guard: This tests record correction, not increased attendance. Use a separate sample-size plan for the correction rate. Do not label every ultrasound or self-check as an up-to-date mammogram.

recommendations.title: Connect the invitation to an observable pathway.
recommendations.text: Reconcile prior examinations, contact details and eligibility. Link sent → delivered → booked → completed with stable identifiers and dates. German reports of outside examinations and the scope of Czech claims data make record checks a sensible first step. [9] [16]
recommendations.metric: Monitor: verified overdue denominator, delivery and completion by invitation round.

recommendations.title: Make the referral pathway understandable.
recommendations.text: Explain the normal referral route and the justified exceptions that centres may handle from July 2026. Give booking staff a consistent script. US ordering evidence motivates reducing steps, but does not prove the Czech policy’s effect. [17] [10]
recommendations.metric: Monitor: referrals unresolved, steps to book, time from contact to appointment.

recommendations.title: Match invitations to real local capacity.
recommendations.text: Check available slots before increasing outreach. A 2024 Czech snapshot found regional waits ranging from 11 to 62 days. These historical figures justify checking current conditions, not assuming the same waits today. [28]
recommendations.metric: Monitor: current wait distribution, unused offered slots and displacement of usual care.

recommendations.title: Keep a human route alongside digital tools.
recommendations.text: Offer phone and accessible communication, with language support where needed. Australian calling evidence is encouraging for booking; translated letters alone were insufficient. Test completion and reach before scaling. [11]
recommendations.metric: Monitor: reach and completed visits by language, age, disability and contact availability.

recommendations.title: Make informed choice part of quality.
recommendations.text: Use balanced information about benefits and harms, explain discomfort honestly, and respect an informed decline. European guidance and pain research support this patient-centred design; attendance should not be the only success measure. [18] [14]
recommendations.metric: Monitor: understanding, distress, informed refusals, complaints and unwanted repeat contacts.

recommendations.title: Learn across invitation rounds.
recommendations.text: Repeated Czech invitations have diminishing response. Preserve randomized comparisons when evaluating new approaches; use prediction to prioritize assistance, not as evidence of why someone did not attend. Validate performance across groups. [1] [19]
recommendations.metric: Monitor: absolute lift, uncertainty, equity, incremental cost and attendance at the next eligible round.
